source: Kuhn (1962) The Structure of Scientific Revolutions, ch. IX (transcription by A. Blunden, marxists.org)
finding: Chapter IX read in full. Kuhn calls crisis a growing sense, often in a narrow part of the community, that the paradigm has stopped working. He gives no count of anomalies. He says the importance of a discovery is often proportional to the extent and stubbornness of the anomaly that foreshadowed it. He lists accuracy of prediction (especially quantitative), balance of esoteric and everyday subject matter, and number of problems solved as useful criteria, with simplicity, scope and compatibility as less useful.
numbers: No numeric threshold anywhere in the chapter. The transcription holds only ch. IX and the 1969 postscript; ch. VII-VIII (crisis, decision to reject) were not available.
quote: the sense of malfunction that can lead to crisis is prerequisite to revolution
limits: One chapter only. Kuhn 1977 (theory choice without rules) was not opened; it is known only through SEP (a01).
agent_relevance: Closes the 'how many anomalies' half of gap 7: Kuhn gives none, so any failure count N is our design choice. His quality criteria (predictive accuracy, problems solved) look more like a progress signal than a counter.

source: Horner & Tung (2011) Playing Cards with Thomas Kuhn: A Critical Reexamination of the Bruner and Postman (1949) Experiment. Review of General Psychology
finding: Two experiments replicated Bruner and Postman. Exp 1 measured reaction times for regular, colour-reversed (trick) and mixed sets. People identified regular and trick cards equally well in pure sets but were slower on the same cards in a mixed set. Exp 2 was a conceptual replication with recognition thresholds and frustration ratings: similar frustration for trick and regular cards, and a systematic trial-and-error strategy for any ambiguous card. The authors say this is inconsistent with resistance to incongruity.
numbers: Abstract read through the Crossref record for DOI 10.1037/a0023597. Sample sizes and thresholds are not in the abstract; the publisher page returned 403.
quote: These findings are inconsistent with an interpretation of resistance to incongruities.
limits: Abstract only. The slowdown in mixed sets is a context-uncertainty effect, not stubbornness. It does not show Kuhn was wrong about science, only that the 1949 cards do not show resistance.
agent_relevance: Closes gap 6: the replication did not reproduce resistance to anomaly. So K01 and K02 (1949 cards) should not be used as evidence that agents or people cling to a frame; support for S6 from that line is weaker than a08 to a10 suggest.

source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy: Imre Lakatos (progressive and degenerating programmes)
finding: A programme is progressive if both theoretically and empirically progressive, and degenerating if not. Theoretically progressive: each new theory has excess empirical content over its predecessor. Empirically progressive: some of the novel predictions are corroborated. Degenerating: successive theories deliver no novel predictions, or the novel predictions are false. No fixed waiting period is given; degenerating programmes can stage a comeback (the Flynn effect reversed a verdict 13 years later).
numbers: No numbers except the 13-year example. About the first 100,000 of 130,627 characters were read.
quote: is progressive if it is both theoretically and empirically progressive, and degenerating if it is not
limits: Secondary source. No operational test in the text.
agent_relevance: A Lakatos signal can be made concrete for an LLM: after a patch, did it predict any new checkable fact, and did that fact hold? That differs from counting failures and avoids dropping a frame whose anomalies are old. No LLM study that tests it was found (gap 9 stays open).

source: Smith (2026) The Little Scientist (arXiv 2608.16951), section 3.4 Kuhn agent
finding: The Kuhn agent fires after a configurable number of consecutive non-improving iterations. It gets the Scientist's instructions but none of its built-up artifacts and no history file, plus an injected paradigm-shifting conjecture and a random cross-disciplinary inspiration. The paper's own note says the ablation found this structure non-load-bearing against a simple control statement. The value of N is not stated in the text.
numbers: 63 Kuhn runs, 33.5M tokens, 531K tokens per run (Table 1), of 229.0M total.
quote: The ablation study negated this structure as non-load bearing vs a simple control statement.
limits: No arm isolates the Kuhn agent. N is not reported, so there is no dose information.
agent_relevance: Gaps 1 and 2 stay open. The one fresh-context trigger in the literature had no N sweep. Fresh context with no history is the part to isolate and test.

source: Smith (2026) The Little Scientist, sections 5.2-5.3 (loop vs one-shot bandit nulls)
finding: Each loop arm is compared with the best of 15 fresh one-shot draws from the same model and prompt (equal number of evaluations). Two null pools: H (n=114, mean 0.7644, sd 0.0736) and HG (n=88, mean 0.7802, sd 0.0659). Expected best-of-15 is 0.8463 (H) and 0.8455 (HG). Seven of ten arms (B, C, D, E, G, I, K) do not beat the HG one-shot bandit; the full scaffold B (top mean 0.8027) is below both pools. Only arm L (floor prompt, keep-if-better) clears both (0.8906).
numbers: B uses 111.4M tokens per run vs 15M for fifteen fresh pulls (7-8x). Pairwise power at n=10 per arm: minimum detectable gap 0.063; the L vs G gap of 0.029 has 26% power. Monte-Carlo SE near band edges 0.005-0.01.
quote: A rising within-run score curve is not by itself evidence of within-run learning
limits: One task (DNA motif discovery), one model family, n=10 per arm. The Kuhn side-agents were one of five changes made together in Phase 2; no arm drops only the Kuhn agent.
agent_relevance: Best-of-N at equal evaluations is a hard baseline: most elaborate loops lose to it. A frame-switch trigger must be tested against it at equal tokens. For this loop the scaffold did not beat blind resampling, and the trigger was never tested alone (gap 1 open).

source: Smith (2026) The Little Scientist, Phase 1 stall and its cause
finding: Phase 1 ended after 49 consecutive runs with zero accepted improvements. The authors trace the stall to infrastructure: a synthetic benchmark that did not match real performance, and per-instance diagnostics deleted before the agent could read them. Reframing would have been reframing the wrong objective.
numbers: Phase 1: 236 evaluated iterations, 1,588 invocations, 97.6M tokens. Phase 2 reached 0.846 in 10 days with 97.9M tokens.
limits: Single case study; the causal story is the authors' own.
agent_relevance: A plateau has several causes (bad signal, blind agent, wrong frame). A trigger should check signal health before blaming the frame.

source: Park & Choi (2026) When Do Agent Loops Mistake Stagnation for Progress? (arXiv 2607.25152)
finding: Controlled pilot with one frontier agent and three evaluator arrangements, changing only what the evaluator is grounded in. The agent claimed improvement in all 54 cycles, but 56% had a measured delta of zero or below. A self-verdict gate became accept-all and eroded the best deployed state by 19%. The strongest in-band judge (full artifact, diff, verdict history) accepted cycles of which 44% were real regressions and rejected 38% of real improvements. On a task whose success is checkable from the artifact itself, the judge's mirage fell to 0.
numbers: 54 cycles; 56% zero-or-negative; 19% erosion; 44% regressions accepted; 38% improvements rejected; sign-only feedback gave similar output (mean 110.0 vs 113.0 with full feedback).
quote: scaling up the judge is not enough; out-of-band evaluation with access to the real world is a structural requirement
limits: Preprint by independent authors, self-described preliminary pilot, one agent, simulated user world.
agent_relevance: Gap 3, in direction: a trigger built on the agent's own verdicts will misfire both ways. Count failures from an external signal (tests, verifier, measured delta). A bare accept/reject verdict from outside was enough.

source: Park & Choi (2026), sections 3.3 and 3.7 (days-flat rule, frame-adversarial review)
finding: The field design counts how many days a metric has been flat. When stagnation passes a threshold, a mode is forced on in which only real-mechanism changes can be accepted. A frame-adversarial review has the agent list its core assumptions in a registry and, periodically or after consecutive worsening, write for each one the alternative and why to keep or drop it. The authors say these are design notes not validated by their measurement.
numbers: No measured effect for the frame review or the threshold. Basis: one 61-cycle, six-week deployment.
limits: Not validated; the authors say its efficacy is capped by model capability.
agent_relevance: A concrete spec for a trigger that is outcome-based (days flat), registry-based (core assumptions only, supports gap 4) and forces an alternative to be named (gap 5). Unmeasured, so a design candidate only.

source: Alderete et al. (2026) Separable Pathways for Causal Reasoning (arXiv 2604.20039), trigger design
finding: The regime-change monitor (DB4) first checks that at least 10 steps have passed and that it has not fired. It then sends the last 5 messages, the state graph and a summary to Haiku 4.5 asking whether the agent has found a rule that worked for several trials but then stopped. It fires if the 0-10 score is at least 6.0. On firing it adds a reflection state telling the agent to count prior successes and re-test under the new regime. It fires at most once per episode.
numbers: Score threshold 6.0; minimum 10 steps; one firing per episode. Acting model Sonnet 4.5, judge Haiku 4.5; n=110 per agent pooled over three batches.
limits: The trigger is itself an LLM judgement of the transcript, not an external failure count. One model family. Repeated firing untested.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: this trigger is self-judged, and nobody compared it with an external signal. Its benefit was avoiding early submission, not accuracy.

source: Alderete et al. (2026), results on reasoning eligibility
finding: Exactly-N episodes are those where the agent submits exactly at the switch threshold, before seeing post-switch evidence. The context-graph agent hit exactly-N in 28.0% (14/50) vs 6.0% (3/50) with the monitor (Fisher p=0.003, OR 6.09, Cohen's h 0.62). Base vs monitor, 14.0% vs 6.0%, was not significant (p=0.159). Among reasoning-eligible episodes, context-graph agent 93.9% vs bare LLM 73.3% (p=0.038). The context-graph agent reached the switch in 94% of episodes vs 74% for Base.
numbers: Raw accuracy: Base 87.3%, CG 77.3% (p=0.077). All 33 'A,B' errors fall in exactly-N episodes. No reasoning-eligible episode submitted the pre-switch answer.
limits: Synthetic blicket-style task; 11+ iterated runs raise the risk of overfitting (the authors' own caveat).
agent_relevance: Detecting the change was not the bottleneck once agents saw post-switch evidence; the loss came from submitting too early. Blocking commitment right after a regime change is what helped.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Thoughts Are All Over the Place (arXiv 2501.18585), TIP results
finding: A thought-switching penalty (TIP) lowers switching and raises accuracy on AIME2024: QwQ-32B-Preview pass@1 38.3 to 44.1; R1-Distill-Qwen-32B 61.4 to 64.1; DeepSeek-R1 73.8 to 74.8. For R1, switch tokens fall from 13.8 to 5.7 and the mean interval rises from 580.1 to 941.6 tokens. Strength 3 with duration 600 was chosen. At strength 20, durations beyond 300 hurt, so too much persistence also fails.
numbers: Tuning example: at strength 3, duration 300 to 600 raised accuracy 35.2% to 39.8%.
limits: Decoding-level penalty on open models; AIME2024 has only 30 problems; the gain for the strongest model is +1.0.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: reasoning models already switch, and on math they switch too much. A frame trigger on top of built-in switching is not obviously useful; a minimum commit window beat free switching. Test an added trigger against a switch penalty.

source: Wang et al. (2025), prompt arm and best-of-N stacking
finding: A prompt asking R1 to persist with each idea did not help: 73.8 to 72.4 on AIME2024 (TIP gave 74.8). TIP also stacks with sampling methods: R1-Distill with laconic decoding at 16 samples went from 72.3 to 77.5 with TIP; R1 with self-consistency stayed near 73.8 and moved to 74.8 with TIP.
numbers: Table 4: 10,000 trials resampled from 32 responses per problem.
limits: Resampling from a fixed pool of 32; one benchmark.
agent_relevance: Persistence worked as a decoding mechanism, not as an instruction. An instruction-only 'stay with it' scaffold may do nothing, so a trigger should be a mechanism such as a forced commit window.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet (arXiv 2310.01798), answer changes and debate
finding: Without oracle labels, GPT-3.5 keeps its first answer 74.7% of the time on GSM8K after two self-correction rounds. Among the changes it more often turns a correct answer into a wrong one than the reverse. GPT-4 and GPT-4-Turbo mostly keep their answers. At equal response counts, self-consistency beats multi-agent debate on GSM8K: 6 responses, 85.3 vs 83.2 for debate round 2.
numbers: Only the 74.7% and the 85.3 vs 83.2 figures were confirmed in the extracted text; the change-rate figure labels were garbled.
quote: The fundamental issue is that LLMs cannot properly judge the correctness of their reasoning.
agent_relevance: Supports gap 3: a self-judged failure signal turns right answers into wrong ones, so a trigger fed by self-verdicts will switch away from correct frames. Sample-and-vote at equal calls is the baseline.

finding: EvoSCM keeps a population of causal-model hypotheses and turns discrepancies into correction rules. Full system 75.09% explanation accuracy. Free-form textual hypotheses 48.18%; random actions 47.45%; free-form SCM rewriting 70.73%; no deduction check 67.09%; no correction rules 66.37%; no pre-committed prediction 63.47%; no latent-state inference 69.58%. Population size K=1 gave 63.27%, K=4 74.86%, K=6 75.09%, K=8 75.01%.
numbers: Normalised MSE: full 2.77e-4, text-only 7.82e-2. Domains: physics, chemistry/materials, biology.
limits: Authors' own system and benchmarks; no replication; the number of failures needed to trigger revision is not studied.
agent_relevance: Supports holding about four competing frames and committing to a prediction before seeing results, which makes a failure unambiguous (gaps 3 and 4). The authors say pre-commitment stops post-hoc rationalising.

source: Yang et al. (2026) Can LLMs Uncover Hidden Physical Laws through Free Exploration? (LongChang, arXiv 2610.37649)
finding: Twelve LLMs explored altered-physics worlds without hints. One model discovered the altered law (16.7%); the other 11 scored 0%. In normal-physics control scenes, 36.1% of reports were rejected for false claims of altered laws or unsupported explanations. Task guidance plus a scene clue raised discovery from 16.7% to 28.6% with evidence support unchanged. Raising turns from 100 to 500 did not help (14.3%). Disabling apparatus cut discovery to 4.8%.
numbers: Tables 3-4 as printed. Model names are as printed in the paper and were not checked elsewhere.
limits: Preprint; LLM judges grade the reports; small scene count.
agent_relevance: Gaps 4 and 5: a trigger that fires on any anomaly also fires on noise (36.1% false anomaly claims). A concrete hint helped more than a bigger budget, mildly supporting offering a candidate frame at the trigger. This differs from Chinn and Brewer's null in people.

source: Gawali (2026) Restart, Don't Persist: Optimal Restart Strategies for Heavy-Tailed LLM Agent Runs (DOI 10.13140/RG.2.2.21690.76483)
finding: Only the title and author were seen, in the DataCite record. The abstract and numbers could not be read (ResearchGate returned 403). The title implies a restart-versus-persist cutoff analysis for runs with heavy-tailed length.
limits: Unread. Do not cite any number from it.
agent_relevance: Possibly the one source on gap 2 (best cutoff). Must be opened before use.
